Record · Walter Hines Page
A house directed
from London.
Garran Hill · 1916
Walter Hines Page · 1855–1918
He named it Garran Hill.
The life he imagined happened elsewhere.

In February 1913, he bought a thousand-acre farm on land his father had logged a generation earlier. He gave it a name before the first stone was laid: Garran Hill.

"Build the farm, therefore; and let me hear at every stage of that happy game."

Weeks later, Wilson offered him London. The ambassadorship to the Court of St. James's. Page accepted — and left. He directed the making of the house by letter, from three thousand miles away, while his son Ralph carried the work on the ground.

When he finally reached Pinehurst in December 1918, the house was finished. He stayed at Currituck Cottage — not Garran Hill — and died there ten days later.

"Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?"

— Aberdeen station · December 11, 1918

The Craftsmen · 1915–1916

Built by the same hands
building Pinehurst.

Leonard Tufts provided the craftsmen -- the same men building Pinehurst. The brickwork, the millwork, seven fireplaces. Every cornice drawn full-size by the architect.

"The friend of Britain in her sorest need."
— Westminster Abbey

Blue Fox · 1946–1965

Her Irish hunter.
Still marked.

The marker reads: MY IRISH HUNTER / BLUE FOX / 1946–1965.
Someone still puts flowers there.

Hollycrest · 1959–1984

Betty Dumaine.
Twenty-five years.

In 1959, Elizabeth Dumaine purchased Hollycrest. She had graduated from the Edith Johnson School in Cambridge. Her Radcliffe roommate was Srinagarindra — who became the Princess Mother of Thailand.

She lived here for twenty-five years. She kept a horse named Blue Fox. She died in 1984. The house stood vacant for nearly fourteen years after.

The Village Heritage Foundation placed a plaque. It reads: Hollycrest. A landmark of exceptional historic significance.
